data.title: Stocktwits Weekly Spread: What Shaped Treasury Yields And The Dollar This Week
data.description:
Key points:
  • An AI-linked equities basket (SOX) dropped 7.2% on Friday, and the Nasdaq 100 ended its worst month since 2025.
  • The U.S. Dollar Index ended flat this week. 
  • The yield curve remained range-bound, with 10-year yields easing by 7 basis points over the previous week.

American sovereign debt surged during the week through Oct. 30, driven by a sharp pullback in tech shares linked to artificial intelligence and expanding corporate credit risk spreads that accelerated safe-haven flows into Treasuries.

Primary revenue channels for major American tech giants are demonstrating initial signs of cooling, even as total corporate artificial intelligence investments approach the $750 billion mark for the year. Intel (INTC) shares slipped on soft Q4 guidance, while Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) missed Q3 analyst expectations.

Meanwhile, costs to protect the debt of numerous U.S. technology heavyweights against default hit fresh record highs Friday. The protection price for Intel bonds for five years surged as much as 22.4 basis points Friday morning to 127.9 basis points a year, Bloomberg reported.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield remained below the 5.00% threshold for the second straight week. The 30-year U.S. Treasury yield remained largely unchanged at 5.31% for the week ending Oct. 30.

The spread between the U.S. 10-year yield and the U.S. 2-year yield ticked marginally higher by 3 basis points to 0.33% in the week.

The iShares 20+ Year Treasury ETF (TLT) ended the week 0.6% higher, its fourth straight week of gains, while the shorter-duration iShares 1-3 year ETF (SHY) added about 0.3%. The slight recovery in the shorter-duration bond ETF may reflect easing short-term inflation pressure; however, markets still factor in one more rate hike in December.

Retail sentiment on TLT and SHY was ‘bullish,’ with ‘high’ message volumes.

Yield Curve & Global Sovereign Markets 

Yield curve flattening trends persisted. However, short-duration yields eased almost in tandem with the long end, keeping the gap between 2-year and 10-year Treasuries compressed.

Corporate credit spreads widened, signaling growing stress in corporate balance sheets. Weak tech results are deepening doubts over the AI borrowing boom even as tech giants boost their capital-spending plans. Companies have borrowed nearly $500 billion so far this year for data centers, chips, and other AI projects, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The total was about $200 billion for all of 2025.

Yet certain mega-cap tech entities have begun addressing escalating debt market anxiety. Oracle Corp., featuring the most heavily traded credit default swaps, recently announced plans to limit upcoming capital infusions to $20 billion over the next few years, helping its credit swaps improve.

International sovereign bond markets followed similar trajectories. German 10-year Bund yields and other major sovereign yields mirrored the U.S. decline, reflecting broad-based global demand for safe-haven assets.

Meanwhile, the Dollar Spot Index was flat this week, extending last week’s weakness against a basket of developed market currencies.

data.title: Crypto exchanges tighten security after $6.3 billion Binance hack
data.description:
Binance lost approximately $6.3 billion from its hot wallets in roughly 20 minutes on October 29, 2026. The rest of the crypto industry is now quietly checking its own locks.

Exchanges are reinforcing their defenses and pushing for faster sharing of threat information. The timing is uncomfortable. Crypto platforms are becoming more embedded in mainstream finance just as the biggest name in the business showed how quickly a vault can be emptied.

The attack began at approximately 20:05 UTC on October 29. Within about 20 minutes, attackers had drained around $6.3 billion in digital assets from the exchange's hot wallets.

Hot wallets are the internet-connected accounts exchanges use to process everyday withdrawals. Think of them as the cash drawer at the front of the store, not the safe in the back. They are convenient, and that convenience makes them a target.

Blockchain analytics firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis, and Elliptic have linked the theft with high confidence to TraderTraitor. That North Korean hacking group is associated with the Lazarus Group, a name that shows up in crypto breach reports with depressing regularity.

The damage could have been worse. Around $3 billion of the stolen assets, mostly the stablecoins USDT and USDC, was frozen on-chain by their issuers, Tether and Circle.

Stablecoin issuers can blacklist specific wallet addresses. Once flagged, the tokens in those addresses become effectively unspendable. In this case, that switch locked up close to half the haul before it could move far.

Binance has pledged to cover all user losses. The exchange is drawing on its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, along with corporate reserves. The combined commitment totals over $6.34 billion, including a $1 billion SAFU reserve.

The exchange temporarily paused withdrawals while it ran security reviews. Deposits stayed open, and Binance said it planned a swift resumption. It also told users that individual balances would not be directly affected.

So far, there is no reported evidence that private keys were leaked.

Kraken said it was watching industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its own defenses.

The loudest message from the sector is about speed. Exchanges are calling for faster sharing of threat intelligence, so that an attack pattern spotted at one platform can be flagged to others before it repeats.

The freeze of roughly $3 billion in stablecoins makes the case on its own. Coordinated, rapid action by Tether and Circle recovered more value than most exchange-level defenses ever could after the fact.

Before this month, the largest crypto theft on record was the roughly $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025. That attack was also tied to North Korean hackers.

The Binance breach is more than four times that size.

The scale also stands out against Binance's own safety net. The exchange's $1 billion SAFU reserve, once pitched as a backstop for exactly this kind of event, covers only a fraction of the loss. The company is leaning heavily on corporate reserves to make users whole.

Prices across major digital assets declined after the breach. The incident also sharpened skepticism about how centralized exchanges handle customer custody.

Binance's pledge to absorb the losses is expected to ease short-term panic. Users who see their balances intact are less likely to rush for the exits.

The stablecoin freeze showed that centrally issued tokens can be a powerful recovery tool when hackers grab them. It also reminded everyone that issuers hold a switch that can lock funds at the address level.

data.title: PRFoods Consolidated Audited Annual Report 2025/2026
data.description:
Management Commentary

In the 2025/2026 financial year, the Group continued to implement the debt restructuring plan agreed in the 2024/2025 financial year. At the end of the financial year, the Group successfully completed its exit from the Saaremaa production unit in Estonia, resulting in a one-off gain of EUR 1.0 million, with total proceeds from the disposal amounting to EUR 2.3 million. The sale of the Saaremaa unit brought the Group’s production activities in Estonia to an end and enables the Group to focus on higher value-added products in the UK market. The Management Board would like to thank the Saaremaa team for their contribution and acknowledge Management Board member Timo Pärn for his work in managing the unit and the Group as a whole.

The table below provides a summary of the Group’s results from discontinued and continuing operations.

The Group’s revenue from the Saaremaa and Scotland production units amounted to EUR 15.3 million, representing a year-on-year decrease of 18.5%. Revenue from the Scotland unit amounted to EUR 13.4 million, down 3.1% compared with the previous year, reflecting weak consumer demand, pricing pressure, tax changes and uncertainty in the retail and HoReCa sectors. Despite challenging market conditions, the Group maintained a strong market position and profitability: the Scotland production unit ended the financial year with an operating profit of EUR 0.1 million (2024/2025: EUR 0.8 million).

The Group ended the 2025/2026 financial year with a loss. The Group’s total net loss from discontinued and continuing operations amounted to EUR 2.5 million. The net loss from discontinued operations was EUR 0.2 million; excluding the one-off gain from the disposal of the production unit, the loss would have amounted to EUR 1.3 million (2024/2025: loss of EUR 1.0 million).

Continuing operations generated a net loss of EUR 2.3 million (2024/2025: net profit of EUR 8.3 million, including a EUR 7.3 million gain from the restructuring of debt obligations). The result was affected by EUR 1.9 million of interest expense recognised on the restructured debt obligations using the effective interest method. The nominal interest rate on the loans is 0% and, in accordance with the restructuring agreement, no interest payments are made, thereby reducing pressure on cash flows and supporting the implementation of the Group’s strategic objectives. The Scotland unit ended the financial year at break-even (2024/2025: profit of EUR 0.5 million).

The Management Board is focused on restoring the profitability of the Scotland unit and improving operational efficiency, with the objective of increasing cash flows, strengthening the Group’s capital position and achieving the targets set out in the restructuring agreement.

We would like to thank all our employees, business partners and investors for their commitment and trust. The restructuring measures implemented have laid the foundation for a stronger Group and ensured the continuation of the Group’s operations.
